subject: literature
passage: Mr. Pennington prided himself upon being a man of independent views, and he was never more conscious of the distinction than at dinner, where he was accustomed to deliver them. On this particular evening he spoke at length upon the folly of the new harbor scheme, the decline of the drama, and the character of the Bishop, and he observed with satisfaction that Mrs. Ashby, who was known to read, had twice nodded. It was only afterward, in the smoking room, when he took up that morning's paper to pass the quarter hour before the carriages came, that his eye fell upon the leading article, and he read, with a sensation he could not immediately name, his three opinions set out in order, in very nearly the words he had used, by a writer he had never met and would, he reflected, have described as a hack.
stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Mr. Pennington's opinions are so widely shared that a journalist has printed them in the newspaper.
choices.B: Mr. Pennington is embarrassed when Mrs. Ashby reveals that she has read the same article he has.
choices.C: Mr. Pennington discovers that the views he believed were his own had been supplied by the morning's newspaper.
choices.D: Mrs. Ashby's nods convince Mr. Pennington that his opinions are well founded.

explanation.why: The text first establishes Mr. Pennington's pride in his "independent views" and his satisfaction in delivering them. The ending undercuts that pride: in "that morning's paper" he finds "his three opinions set out in order, in very nearly the words he had used." The reader is meant to see that he had absorbed the article and repeated it as his own.
explanation.A: Incorrect. This reverses the direction of borrowing: the article was written before dinner, so the newspaper did not print his opinions; he repeated the newspaper's.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Mrs. Ashby reveals nothing; she only nods, and the discovery happens when he is alone in the smoking room.
explanation.C: Correct. The opinions he delivered as his own appear in the morning paper he had evidently read, which is the irony the whole text builds toward.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Her nods are a passing detail of his satisfaction at dinner, not the point of the text.
